blocks.text: Have you ever wondered why a heavy ship floats on water while a small stone sinks?

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore the concepts of upthrust and Archimedes' principle, which explain why objects float or sink in a fluid. Understanding these principles is crucial for applications in engineering, design, and everyday life.

blocks.title: Archimedes' Principle
blocks.text: Archimedes' principle states that any object, wholly or partially immersed in a fluid, experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.

blocks.markdown: The upthrust, also known as buoyant force, is the force that allows objects to float. It acts upwards, opposing the weight of the object. The magnitude of this force is equal to the weight of the fluid that the object displaces. This principle is crucial for understanding flotation.

blocks.title: Calculating Upthrust
blocks.prompt: A block of wood with a volume of 0.5 m³ is submerged in water. Calculate the upthrust acting on the block.

steps.text: Determine the volume of water displaced, which is equal to the volume of the block: 0.5 m³.
Calculate the weight of the displaced water using the density of water (1000 kg/m³) and gravitational acceleration (9.8 m/s²).

blocks.answer: The upthrust acting on the block is 4900 N.

blocks.markdown: Objects float when the upthrust is equal to or greater than their weight. The law of flotation states that a floating object displaces its own weight of fluid. This principle is used to determine the relative density of objects.

blocks.title: Exam Tip
blocks.text: Remember that the apparent loss in weight of an object in a fluid is equal to the upthrust. This concept is often tested in exams.

points: Archimedes' principle explains the concept of upthrust and flotation.
The upthrust is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by an object.
Relative density can be calculated using the apparent loss of weight in a fluid.
